extracted.intended_audience: public speakers, Toastmasters members, and aspiring joke writers/comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, teachable techniques for structuring jokes to add humor to speeches, presentations, or short comedy bits—focused on misdirection, assumption-based twists, and concise punch placement. Includes a 4-step joke-writing process and heuristics for idea generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic element of surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is created when there is a comedic element of surprise: the audience believes one thing to be true, only to have it revealed that something else is actually true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surprise must be a twist without serious repercussions. If the twist seems to have serious consequences listeners may react negatively (e.g., 'That's mean!') instead of laughing. Consider negative feedback valid and soften punches that cause real pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the joke concise so the setup doesn't dilute the twist; brevity increases comedic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim extraneous details; delay the punch as long as possible while keeping the setup clear. The author notes the process may take time to learn but becomes faster with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use misdirection to lull the audience into a particular expectation, creating tension that the twist will release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misdirection makes the twist stronger by leading listeners away from the punch. Example: adding 'The people who live above me are furious...' leads the audience away from thinking about a skylight for star-gazing, making the eventual reveal funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal punch word/phrase at the last possible moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay the punch word or punch phrase until as close to the end as possible to maximize the element of surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'punch word' is the single laugh-triggering word; a 'punch phrase' is a string of words that form the laugh. Place it at the sentence end when possible; use misdirection and conciseness to support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connection between setup and punch
rubrics_metrics.description: The setup and punch line should connect in a logical way, even if the punch reframes the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the twist is believable as a reinterpretation of the setup; purely random twists feel disconnected and flop. Use buildup to make the logical shift satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with truth / factual premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Always begin with a truthful, factual piece of information rather than trying to be funny first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting real pulls the audience in and makes the later surprise more effective; funny-first ideas can be overdone or unbelievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: List multiple assumptions (brainstorm ~10)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have a factual premise, list about 10 likely assumptions the audience will make about that premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with many assumptions gives more interesting choices; each assumption can be probed for alternative meanings that yield joke ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate assumptions to find reinterpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Question each assumed detail until you discover reinterpretations that produce a comedic twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from 'eggs' ask what kinds of eggs exist (ostrich, Easter, chocolate). From 'where' ask if it could be 'in my car' etc. Follow the chain of questioning until a surprising but plausible reinterpretation appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific, recognizable details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific brand names or recognizable details to increase the chance of a laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more recognizable the detail (e.g., 'Cadbury'), the more likely the audience will connect quickly and react. Specificity can strengthen misdirection because listeners bring shared associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical questions to involve the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Word jokes as questions when appropriate because questions engage listeners and can misdirect their thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions invite the audience to imagine a common experience and can set up a punch that reframes that imagined scenario; craft the wording to steer their assumptions where you want them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing a single technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption-twist structure can lose impact if used repetitively and becomes predictable to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary techniques and joke structures; if the audience recognizes the pattern, the element of surprise diminishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience sensitivity and ethical impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should avoid causing real pain; be responsive to feedback that a joke is mean or hurtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a joke targets a vulnerable person/group or causes harm, soften or adjust the punch. Subjectivity in comedy means an otherwise well-structured joke can flop if it offends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Who/What/Where/When/Why/How checklist and attribute prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: While writing, ask Who/What/Where/When/Why/How and probe attributes like gender, location, age, time of day, clothing, quantity, ownership, vehicles, occupations, sound, smell, procedure, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prompts help generate concrete, varied assumptions and details to investigate for reinterpretation and misdirection. The page lists many prompts (gender, location, age, era, clothing, weight, breed, sound, smell, etc.) as idea generators.
